chief_complaint: Empathy drill — responding to a patient's emotions
persona_override: You are a patient in a clinic who is going through a hard time. This is an EMPATHY PRACTICE for a beginner. In EACH of your turns, express ONE emotion or worry in just 1-2 short sentences, then STOP and wait for the student to respond. Examples you can draw from: fear about test results, sadness after bad news, frustration about a long wait, feeling overwhelmed caring for a sick parent, embarrassment about a symptom, worry about money or work. Do NOT ask clinical questions and do NOT give a medical history. React to how the student responds: if they warmly name and acknowledge your feeling, soften and open up a little more; if they ignore the emotion and jump to facts or rush to reassure you, stay upset and say you don't feel heard. Move to a DIFFERENT emotional situation every couple of turns so the student practises several. Keep your turns short. The session ends when the student says "I'd like to end the session."

clinical_knowledge.topic: Empathy drill — responding to a patient's emotions evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Empathy drill — responding to a patient's emotions is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Evidence-based management requires monitoring clinical response to therapy, screening for medication side effects, and reinforcing safety-netting criteria.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Empathy drill — responding to a patient's emotions.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
management_principles: Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
Provide clear patient education, address patient concerns, and establish explicit follow-up and safety-netting instructions.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

learning_objectives: Practise the NURSE skills: Name, Understand, Respect, Support, Explore
Acknowledge emotion before moving to facts or reassurance
Build a bank of natural empathic phrases

phrase_categories.name: NAME — label the feeling
phrases: It sounds like you're feeling really scared.
I can see this is very upsetting for you.
You seem quite frustrated by all of this.

phrase_categories.name: UNDERSTAND — show it makes sense
phrases: I can understand why this would worry you.
Anyone in your situation would feel the same.
That makes complete sense to me.

phrase_categories.name: RESPECT — acknowledge their strength
phrases: You've been dealing with a lot.
It took courage to come in and talk about this.
You're handling this better than you think.

phrase_categories.name: SUPPORT — offer partnership
phrases: You're not alone in this — I'm here to help.
Let's take it one step at a time.

phrase_categories.name: EXPLORE — invite more
phrases: Can you tell me more about what's worrying you most?
What's been the hardest part for you?
Would you like to say more about that?
